posts.original_html: I put the Rancho 4/2 lift on my truck 2 years ago, along with 32x11.50 BFG's. I still use the same 15 x 10 hurricanes that it had to begin with. I sometimes get offroad with it, but the biggest reason was because I was tired of how low the stock 2wd stance was. Starting off, the truck had 2" drop shackles in the rear and was rolling on 295/50 BFG's. After the lift, going from the low profile tires to where its at now, the total lift at the end was 7" front and 4" rear. I put the stock rear shackles back on, getting rid of the drop shackles it used to have. A year ago, I geared the it down from the stock 3.42's to 4.11's. BIG DIFFERENCE. Alot more snap now, and it also gets 2mpg better gas mileage than before the geardown, putting it back around what it was before I started the lift. I can't figure how to upload an image here, I was going to put a before & after up to show the difference, send an email if you'd like to see.
posts.rewritten_content:
I installed the Rancho 4/2 lift on my truck two years ago, along with 32x11.50 BFG tires. The original stock rear shackles were replaced with drop shackles initially, using 295/50 BFGs. After the lift, the total front lift is 7 inches and the rear lift is 4 inches. I reverted to the stock rear shackles after lifting.

A year ago, I changed the gear ratio from stock 3.42s to 4.11s, which significantly improved acceleration and increased fuel efficiency by about 2 mpg, bringing it back close to its original performance levels.

I intended to include before-and-after photos but can send you an email if you'd like to see them.

threads.title: Finding Out If Your Vehicle Has A Recall Is Very Easy

ai_article.rewritten_title: How to Check if Your Vehicle Has an Outstanding Recall
ai_article.summary: This thread provides a method for checking vehicle recalls using the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN). It also discusses limitations and what can't be checked through this process.
seo_outline: Introduction to recalling vehicles and why it’s important
How to use VIN to check for recalls
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
Checking if your vehicle has an outstanding recall is a straightforward process. Members in this thread provide assistance by running their vehicle's VIN through General Motors (GM) systems at work or with other professionals who have access to such data. However, it’s important to note that the system may not have records for vehicles older than 10 years.

TRITON20 initially offered to check VINS and provide recall information but stated he was no longer able to do so due to restrictions at work. Others in the thread mentioned continuing this tradition by working at dealerships, suggesting you can still post your VIN here for others to check if they have access to these systems.

According to TRITON20, running a vehicle's VIN through GM’s system allows checking for outstanding recalls but does not provide information on other service history such as damage from accidents or floods. For instance, he explained that the recall related to tailgate cable replacement was completed in June 2005 under recall number 04007.

Some members posted their VINS and received recall confirmations or negative results. TRITON20 also mentioned that vehicles older than 92-93 might not be viewable due to them being deleted from GM’s data base.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Rear End Ratio Codes and Their Meanings
ai_article.summary: This thread provides a list of RPO codes for different rear end ratios in Chevrolet trucks, including their meanings and locations. Users discuss the presence of these codes in their vehicles.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
The thread provides a list of RPO codes for different rear end ratios in Chevrolet trucks. The codes include GQ1, GT4, GT5, GU4, GU5, GU6, and G80. These codes can be found on the bottom of a sticker inside the glovebox.

These are some of the codes:
- **GQ1**: AXLE REAR, STD RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GT4**: AXLE REAR, 3.73 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GT5**: AXLE REAR, 4.10 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GU4**: AXLE REAR, 3.08 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GU5**: AXLE REAR, 3.23 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GU6**: AXLE REAR, 3.42 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **G80**: AXLE REAR, LIMITED SLIP (POSITRACTION) (Post ID: 2755)

Users also discuss the presence of a code for a 4.56 ratio in military trucks (Post ID: 2763).

Regarding the G80 code, users are unsure if it indicates a gear ratio or a locking differential function (Post IDs: 2759, 2761, 2762, 2764, 2765, 2766). Brendan explains that G80 is for the limited slip, not the ratio (Post ID: 2764).

Another user mentions that G80 works well in their vehicle but others report issues with it locking inconsistently (Post IDs: 2769, 2771, 2773, 2775).

ai_article.summary: This project focuses on the frame and suspension modifications of a Suburban, including removing old cross members and installing new ones with improved reinforcement. The build aims to provide enhanced articulation capabilities.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This project focuses on the frame and suspension modifications of a Suburban, including removing old cross members and installing new ones with improved reinforcement. The build aims to provide enhanced articulation capabilities.

The back of the truck had three cross members that were all in the way. With a panhard mount, shock mounts, winch mount, relocated gas tank mounts, and general frame strengthening support needed, it all had to come out and be redesigned.

Old x-members:
![](http://i14.photobucket.com/albums/a307/bonedust213/truck/post-1-0-45016800-1295303656_thumb.jpg)

And removed:
![](http://i14.photobucket.com/albums/a307/bonedust213/truck/post-1-0-09137000-1295303761_thumb.jpg)

The frame was plated in where the new x-member will live. The front and back of the frame were tied together using L-shaped gussets.
![](http://i14.photobucket.com/albums/a307/bonedust213/truck/post-1-0-15558600-1295303790_thumb.jpg)

A new x-member, including a panhard mount, was fabricated and installed.
![](http://i14.photobucket.com/albums/a307/bonedust213/truck/post-1-0-80473800-1295303862_thumb.jpg)

The x-member was test fitted to show how the pass-throughs for body mounts work.
![](http://i14.photobucket.com/albums/a307/bonedust213/truck/post-1-0-82933000-1295304906_thumb.jpg)

The x-member was fully welded in and the rear suspension components were installed, including one rear link and a radius arm.

ai_article.rewritten_title: 88GMCtruck's 98 Silverado Tow Pig Build: 'Black Fox'
ai_article.summary: This thread details the restoration and modification process of an 1998 Silverado K3500 tow truck, including a transmission rebuild, exterior upgrades, and interior improvements.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
In 2013, [88GMCtruck](#user) initiated a project to restore an 1998 Silverado K3500 tow truck, which he named 'Black Fox'. The truck was purchased with approximately 135,000 miles and had six new Load E Toyo Open Country AT Tires. [88GMCtruck](#user) noted that the truck's transmission had bearing issues but managed to get it for a reduced price of $5,600 after negotiations.

[88GMCtruck](#user) detailed several modifications planned for 'Black Fox', including rebuilding the transmission with new clutch and bearings, installing towing mirrors, wiring in a trailer plug, and cleaning the paint. Additionally, various parts such as gloveboxes, u-joints, front windows, and HVAC systems were replaced or updated.

The transmission rebuild process involved significant work, including removing and reassembling several components like the input shaft, countershaft, and shift collar. The truck underwent a full restoration, with improvements to both the exterior and interior. [88GMCtruck](#user) also shared details about parts sourced from another project vehicle and junkyard finds.

The final stages included installing heated mirrors, front Kodiak handles, and de-badging the truck. [Scott Long](#user) later inquired about fuel efficiency, to which [88GMCtruck](#user) confirmed good overall performance with a 12.8 MPG on long-distance trips.

This project showcases [88GMCtruck](#user)'s dedication and skill in restoring classic trucks for towing purposes.

So, The story goes like this: I've been looking for a new towpig awhile now. I was looking into duramax trucks but I still wanted a manual. After a few months of searching, etc I determined that the cost of owning one VS how much I would use it and the distances I would go just wasn't worth the money. I'd be buying it and wouldn't have any play money to customize it or anything either. So I started looking for GMT400 trucks again.... I ran across this truck about 3.5 hours from me. 1-owner trade in. The dealership listed it as an auto so I hadn't caught it prior. I called, got the pictures, etc etc.... Got the financing figured out. They were asking $9,000, I got them down to bluebook at $7,600 after pointing out some flaws I could see in the pictures. It also has 6 brand new Load E Toyo Open Country AT Tires.

I take the time to drive down there, with money in hand and a friend to drive my 02 back. I took it for a spin and after a few stoplights noticed a whining sound in gears 1 & 2. posts.rewritten_content:
What an eventful weekend! I spent Friday night reassembling my truck, including installing the transmission and bleeding the clutch. A test drive went smoothly, but 5th gear was problematic; it would grind every time. Upon further investigation, I realized I had installed the shift collar for 5th gear incorrectly, preventing proper engagement with the synchro. Disappointing though this was, at least I only needed to拆卸变速箱、分动箱和传动轴。Saturday morning saw me disassembling again to correct the mistake.

Here’s a visual of my initial installation and how it should have been:

![](images/collar_installed.jpg)
![](images/correct安装方式.jpg)

The taper side features teeth that engage with the synchro, which is crucial for smooth gear changes. After reassembly, everything worked as expected. The transmission now shifts smoothly.

I took a 250-mile trip to break in the truck and achieved an impressive 12.8 MPG at highway speeds between 70-80 MPH. Not bad at all!

Upon returning home, I tackled some updates:

- Replaced tailgate cables with solid straps for added security.
- Installed a center console in place of the rear armrest, which was cheaply priced at $3.74.
- Acquired steering wheel audio controls and an HVAC system with rear defrost.

I also removed wheels to paint them black, installed chrome caps, and removed trim rings for now. Lastly, I fitted power heated signal/parking light tow mirrors and front Kodiak handles (rear ones awaited door rods). The truck is now de-badged as well.

More modifications are on the horizon, including window tinting, light smoking, and deciding on headlight treatments.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Truck Through Its Stages: A Journey from Stock to Beast
ai_article.summary: This thread chronicles the transformation of a truck through various modifications, including suspension lifts, tire changes, and engine upgrades. The journey highlights the owner's progression in customization over several years.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This truck has undergone many changes since its purchase. Initially, it was just a stock vehicle with front tint (Post ID: 255). 

Over time, the owner installed a 3-inch lift (Post ID: 255) and added 17x8 Weld Mountain Crusher rims with BFG ATs (Post ID: 255). After getting bored of this setup, they added a SuperLift lift with 5.5 rear blocks (Post ID: 255), followed by 37-inch BFG MT tires and 4.56 gears along with a Tru-Trac differential (Post ID: 255).

Further modifications included a shackle flip, AAL, and additional tuning (Post ID: 255). The owner then added a 2-inch block to increase clearance (Post ID: 255), leading to the installation of 39.5-inch IROK tires with 5.13 gears, long tube headers, a mild tune, and a Magnaflow muffler with dumps (Post ID: 255).

Due to legal issues, the truck was reduced in height by installing 36-inch IROK tires with Chevy tails for legality (Post ID: 255). The owner then focused on making it faster, adding a TSP220 cam, Circle D 3200 stall, TBSS intake, BB Auto Cal tune, and cat along with Magnaflow muffler to reduce noise (Post ID: 255).

Air bags were installed to raise the truck by 4 inches for special occasions (Post ID: 255). Currently, the owner has a PatG spec'd/EPS ground 223/226 camshaft with TEA .660 dual springs and titanium retainers. They also have a Circle D 36-3700 stall and nitrous system ready for installation (Post ID: 255).

Future plans include adding a Ford HP D60 front end when funds are available (Post ID: 255). The owner is undecided whether to return the truck to 40-inch tires or keep it on 36-37 inches with wider rims and flares (Post ID: 255).

The truck was also plasti-dipped for a chrome look, but some areas still need attention (Post ID: 255).

Since purchasing the truck new, I've gone through multiple setups. Initially, it had stock tires until I installed 3 BL after 7000k. I later added 17x8 Weld Mountain Crusher rims with 285 BFG ATs and Ford keys, along with 4 rear blocks.

After getting bored of that setup, I added a SuperLift lift and 5.5 rear blocks, switching to 37 BFG MTs, 4.56 gears, and a Tru-Trac. I performed a shackle flip, AAL, and dialed in the suspension.

Deciding to go bigger, I upgraded to 2" blocks for a taller stance, installed 39.5 Iroks, 5.13 gears, long tube headers, a mild tune, and a Magnaflow muffler with dumps. Due to frequent police harassment, I downgraded to 36" Iroks with Chevy tails for legality.

To improve ride height, I added 2" blocks with zero rate and tow mirrors. Currently, the truck runs on Pro Comp 17x9 rims. Chrome plasti-dip has been applied to the front grill, but not yet to the bumpers.

Frustrated by the low stance, I upgraded to a TSP220 cam, Circle D 3200 stall, TBSS intake, BB Auto Cal tune, and added a cat along with Bullet/Magnaflow mufflers. Air bags allow for an additional 4" lift when needed.

Recently, I swapped in a PatG spec'd/EPS ground 223/226 cam, TEA .660 dual springs with titanium retainers. A Circle D 36-3700 stall and nitrous kit are ready to be installed once funds permit.

Currently using an HP D60 for the front end, I plan to install SAS when funds allow. Future plans include either going back to 40" tires with wide rims and flares or staying on 36-37"s with wider rims. Updates will be shared as new modifications are made.

ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This project focuses on the frame and suspension modifications of a Suburban, including removing old cross members and installing new ones with improved reinforcement. The build aims to provide enhanced articulation capabilities.

The back of the truck had three cross members that were all in the way. With a panhard mount, shock mounts, winch mount, relocated gas tank mounts, and general frame strengthening support needed, it all had to come out and be redesigned.

ai_article.rewritten_title: 88GMCtruck's 98 Silverado Tow Pig Build: 'Black Fox'
ai_article.summary: This thread details the restoration and modification process of an 1998 Silverado K3500 tow truck, including a transmission rebuild, exterior upgrades, and interior improvements.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
In 2013, [88GMCtruck](#user) initiated a project to restore an 1998 Silverado K3500 tow truck, which he named 'Black Fox'. The truck was purchased with approximately 135,000 miles and had six new Load E Toyo Open Country AT Tires. [88GMCtruck](#user) noted that the truck's transmission had bearing issues but managed to get it for a reduced price of $5,600 after negotiations.

[88GMCtruck](#user) detailed several modifications planned for 'Black Fox', including rebuilding the transmission with new clutch and bearings, installing towing mirrors, wiring in a trailer plug, and cleaning the paint. Additionally, various parts such as gloveboxes, u-joints, front windows, and HVAC systems were replaced or updated.

The transmission rebuild process involved significant work, including removing and reassembling several components like the input shaft, countershaft, and shift collar. The truck underwent a full restoration, with improvements to both the exterior and interior. [88GMCtruck](#user) also shared details about parts sourced from another project vehicle and junkyard finds.

The final stages included installing heated mirrors, front Kodiak handles, and de-badging the truck. [Scott Long](#user) later inquired about fuel efficiency, to which [88GMCtruck](#user) confirmed good overall performance with a 12.8 MPG on long-distance trips.

This project showcases [88GMCtruck](#user)'s dedication and skill in restoring classic trucks for towing purposes.

Additional tasks included cleaning the transfer case and updating trailer and vehicle fluids. Tow mirror parts were also sourced from a friend’s stolen truck, with the passenger side being needed for parts only.

With the mainshaft to be rebuilt, I'll focus on other necessary repairs like the trailer harness and other fluids over the next few days.

What an eventful weekend! I spent Friday night reassembling my truck, including installing the transmission and bleeding the clutch. A test drive went smoothly, but 5th gear was problematic; it would grind every time. Upon further investigation, I realized I had installed the shift collar for 5th gear incorrectly, preventing proper engagement with the synchro. Disappointing though this was, at least I only needed to拆卸变速箱、分动箱和传动轴。Saturday morning saw me disassembling again to correct the mistake.

Here’s a visual of my initial installation and how it should have been:

![](images/collar_installed.jpg)
![](images/correct安装方式.jpg)

The taper side features teeth that engage with the synchro, which is crucial for smooth gear changes. After reassembly, everything worked as expected. The transmission now shifts smoothly.

I took a 250-mile trip to break in the truck and achieved an impressive 12.8 MPG at highway speeds between 70-80 MPH. Not bad at all!

Upon returning home, I tackled some updates:

- Replaced tailgate cables with solid straps for added security.
- Installed a center console in place of the rear armrest, which was cheaply priced at $3.74.
- Acquired steering wheel audio controls and an HVAC system with rear defrost.

I also removed wheels to paint them black, installed chrome caps, and removed trim rings for now. Lastly, I fitted power heated signal/parking light tow mirrors and front Kodiak handles (rear ones awaited door rods). The truck is now de-badged as well.

More modifications are on the horizon, including window tinting, light smoking, and deciding on headlight treatments.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Swapping from NBS 4.3 to V8: Key Components and Considerations
ai_article.summary: This thread provides comprehensive guidance on swapping a NBS 4.3 engine with various V8 engines (4.8/5.3, 5.7) in a 2001 Silverado truck, focusing on components that require modification or replacement.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
When considering swapping a NBS 4.3 engine with a V8 (4.8/5.3 or 5.7) in your 2001 Silverado truck, several components require modification or replacement. Here's what you need to know based on the information provided by experienced users and experts in this forum thread.

**Wiring Harnesses:**
- For swaps involving a 4.8/5.3 V8, any stock wiring harness from this engine family will work fine (Post ID: 3221). A new harness is required if swapping to a 5.7 LS1 (Post IDs: 3221, 3224).
- Customized wiring harnesses are recommended when using 5.7 accessories with 4.8/5.3 mounts and intake systems (Post ID: 3224).

**Radiator:**
The existing radiator is compatible with the V8 engines (Post ID: 3221). However, it might be a good idea to upgrade it (Post IDs: 3221, 3227).

**Powertrain Control Module (PCM):**
The stock 4.3 PCM can be reflashed or replaced with a used one at around $300 (Post ID: 3221). New PCMs are also an option (Post IDs: 3221, 3227).

**Belt Accessories and Mounts:**
- If using components from the same V8 family, not all belt accessories need to be replaced (Post ID: 3221).
- When switching to a 5.7 LS1 with 4.8/5.3 bracketry, new belt accessories are necessary (Post ID: 3221).

**Fuel Pump:**
The existing fuel pump is compatible and does not require replacement (Post ID: 3221).

**Driveshaft:**
The driveshaft remains unchanged in all scenarios; no modifications needed (Post ID: 3221).

**Intake System:**
The stock intake system will not work, necessitating the purchase of an aftermarket intake (Post ID: 3221).

**Transmission Compatibility:**
- The stock transmission can function with a few adjustments. A new converter may be required for certain setups (Post ID: 3222).
- Proper programming or reprogramming is essential to ensure the transmission's longevity (Post IDs: 3224, 3227).

**Engine Mounts and Registers:**
The stock engine mounting locations need modifications or additional supports (Post ID: 3221).

**Exhaust System:**
A complete new exhaust system is required regardless of the V8 chosen (Post IDs: 3221, 3237).

In summary, while some components can be reused from your NBS 4.3 setup, many aspects like wiring harnesses and accessories will need to be updated or replaced for a seamless swap to a V8 engine.

posts.original_html:
I see this question come up alot on this board and others, so I thought that my real world experiences would help out anyone considering swapping a NBS 4.3 to a NBS v8. I will update this again when the actual swap happens.

Truck:
2001 Silverado base model reg cab

Stock Engine/tranny:
2001 4.3 V6 / 4L60E

New Engine / tranny:
2001 LS1 5.7 V8 / 4L60E

I bought the LS1 minus a couple of key items: Wiring Harness, Alternator, A/C compressor, and Electric fans. Know from the start that all this info, unless otherwise noted, works for swaps from the 4.3 to 4.8/5.3/5.7.

Now some comments always seem to come up when people ask about doing this swap:

Question:
I'm swapping to a 4.8/5.3...Do I need a new wiring harness?
Answer:
Yes.

Question:
I'm swapping to a 5.7 LS1...Do I need a new wiring harness?
Answer:
Yes.


Question:
I'm swapping to a 4.8/5.3...Does the wiring harness have to be custom made?
Answer:
No. any stock wiring harness from a 4.8/5.3 will work fine and is fairly priced at about 400. the 5.7 wiring harness will not work, though. will not plug into the truck.

Question:
I'm swapping to a 5.7 LS1 and using LS1 accessories...Does the wiring harness have to be custom made?
Answer:
Yes. due to the location of the alt and the injector plug, a 4.8/5.3 wiring harness will have to be modified to fit. A custom made wiring harness would be easier to use here.

Question:
I'm swapping to a 5.7 LS1 and using 4.8/5.3 accessories...Does the wiring harness have to be custom made?
Answer:
No. any stock wiring harness from a 4.8/5.3 will work fine and is fairly priced at about 400. the 5.7 wiring harness will not work, though. will not plug into the truck.

Question:
Do I need to change out my radiator?
Answer:
No. the 4.3 has 28" radiator like the 5.3. but it's not a terrible idea to upgrade.

Question:
Do I need a new PCM?
Answer:
No, the 4.3 PCM can be reflashed. but if you search for it, you can find package deals of used PCMs and wiring harnesses for around 300.

Question:
I'm swapping to a 4.8/5.3...Do I need all new belt accessories?
Answer:
Only have a partial answer here...but NO, not all of them.

Question:
I'm swapping to a 5.7 LS1 and using 5.7 bracketry and intake...Do I need all new belt accessories?
Answer:
YES. you need all 5.7 accessories.

Question:
I'm swapping to a 5.7 LS1 and using 4.8/5.3 bracketry and intake...Do I need all new belt accessories?
Answer:
Only have a partial answer here...but NO, not all of them.

Question:
Do i need to replace the Fuel Pump?
Answer:
No. it is the same part.

Question:
Will the driveshaft have to be modified?
Answer:
No.

Question:
Will the stock intake system work?
Answer:
No. I'm having to buy an aftermarket intake system to get this done.

Question:
Will the stock tranny work?
Answer:
This is a big question. the stock tranny WILL work. the bell housing is slightly different, but will mate up to the 5.7

Question:
Will the stock engine mounting locations work?
Answer:
no, you'll have to secure some 4.8/5.3L mounts and registers.

Question:
Will the stock exhaust system work?
Answer:
No. you'll either have to remake the entire system or get a 4.8/5.3/6.0 system.

so...if you are considering a swap to a V8, here's what you need:

swap to a 4.8/5.3:
complete engine
belt accessories brackets
4.8/5.3 engine mounts
4.8/5.3 wiring harness
new exhaust system
4.8/5.3 intake system
new PCM or reflash 4.3

swap to a 5.7 LS1 and keeping 5.7 intake and acessories:
complete engine
belt accessories and brackets
4.8/5.3 engine mounts
custom built wiring harness
new exhaust system
new PCM or reflash 4.3

swap to a 5.7 LS1 and using 4.8/5.3 accessories:
complete engine
belt accessories brackets

posts.rewritten_content:
When considering swapping a NBS 4.3 to a NBS v8, such as a 2001 Silverado base model with a 4.3 V6 and 4L60E transmission, here are key points based on real-world experience:

- **Wiring Harness**: For swaps from the 4.3 to 4.8/5.3, any stock wiring harness will work; they are priced around $400. A 5.7 LS1 wiring harness won't fit and requires custom modifications if used with a 4.8/5.3.
- **Alternator, Compressor, Fans**: These need to be sourced separately for both the 4.8/5.3 and the 5.7 swaps.
- **Radiator**: The stock radiator is compatible with the 5.3, but upgrading might be beneficial.
- **PCM**: The 4.3 PCM can be reflashed; used PCMs and harnesses are available for about $300.
- **Belt Accessories**: Only partial replacement is needed for a 4.8/5.3 swap; all new accessories are required for the 5.7 LS1, especially with 5.7 bracketry and intake.
- **Fuel Pump**: Remains the same as the original.
- **Driveshaft**: No modifications are necessary.
- **Intake System**: An aftermarket system is needed due to compatibility issues.
- **Transmission**: The stock transmission will work; specific mounts need adjustment for a 5.7 LS1, and an aftermarket intake is required.

In summary, while some components require custom or complete replacements, the swap from a 4.3 to a 4.8/5.3/5.7 V8 can be manageable with proper preparation and parts sourcing.

ai_article.rewritten_title: How to Get Rid of Steering Slop on Your Cutlass Using Intermediate Shaft from Jeep Cherokee
ai_article.summary: This thread details the process of using intermediate shafts from a mid-90's Jeep Cherokee or Grand Cherokee in place of the original rag joint to reduce steering slop in a Cutlass. The author and others share tips on installation, adjustment, and compatibility.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This thread details the process of using intermediate shafts from a mid-90's Jeep Cherokee or Grand Cherokee in place of the original rag joint to reduce steering slop in a Cutlass. The author and others share tips on installation, adjustment, and compatibility.

### Introduction and Problem
Shwa Kid describes his experience with reducing steering slop in his truck by replacing the intermediate shaft from a mid-90's Jeep Cherokee or Grand Cherokee. The original rag joint is known to cause slop, while the intermediate shaft has universals at both ends (Post ID: 4245).

### Intermediate Shaft Installation
The author suggests that the shaft can be installed almost directly into the Cutlass after shaving a small amount from the steering column end to clear the retaining bolt. The shaft may require some heat to compress it during removal or installation. There are alternative methods such as dropping the steering box (Post ID: 4245).

### Steering Box Adjustment
The next step involves adjusting the steering box back to its original condition by first removing it from the truck. The author explains how to remove the retaining ring and adjust the bearing preload, ensuring proper overcentre position to achieve optimal torque readings (14 in-lbs) using an in-lbs torque wrench (Post ID: 4245).

### Compatibility and Further Information
There is some debate about whether the D-shaped part of the column needs a notch or not. The author mentions that there are two types of shafts, with cast ends and bent steel varieties. A notch may be required for proper fitment (Post ID: 4250). Mc87ss provides detailed instructions on how to notch the steering column shaft correctly (Post ID: 4251).

### Notes
Some posts suggest that the universals are not easily rebuildable and recommend sourcing from junkyards. The Borgeson replacement shaft is mentioned as a more expensive alternative (Post IDs: 4258, 4260).

posts.original_html:
Hey guys, I'm in the process of modding/overhauling my truck and in the process making it negotiate corners a little (LOT) better. I keep seeing posts about people trying to get rid of steering slop and either giving up or spending a bunch of money on a new box. Here's what I did, grand total was about $20.

First thing I did was get rid of the slop in the intermediate shaft caused by the old, worn out rag joint. After reading on some G-body forums, my buddy found out that the intermediate shaft from a mid 90's Jeep Cherokee (and some Grand Cherokees) will fit directly into his Cutlass. These shafts have a universal at each end, rather than a universal and a rag joint. We went to the junkyard and picked one up to put in his car but before he put it in, I test fit it in my truck. It fit almost perfectly. The only modification required was to shave a little (like a couple millimeters) from the steering column end to clear the retaining bolt for the intermediate shaft. After a couple km's we decided the shaft was in sub par condition and went back to get another pair (one for each of us). Over the course of the day, we pulled about 4 shafts and kept 2, so make sure the universals are good before you buy the shaft.

The shaft can be a little hard to remove as sometimes you have to heat them to get them to compress if they've been sitting. We found the easiest way to remove the shaft is to unbolt each end, then remove the steering column (2 15mm bolts) and just throttle it (the steering column) until it (the steering shaft) disconnects at the top, then just slide the bottom off. Alternative method would be to drop the steering box and get it off that way. It helps to be able to steer the vehicle so you can access the retaining bolts, luckily these vehicles weren't exactly hard to defeat should you not have a key.

Here's some pics of the shaft in my truck.



The next thing I did to tighten my steering was adjust the steering box back to it's original condition. First step of this is to remove the steering box from the truck. A ball joint removal tool really helps to remove the centre link, but it's not totally necessary if you're proficient with a pickle fork. Be careful when removing the lines as you really don't want to strip them.
Once you have the box out, drain all of the fluid.

Setting Bearing Preload: Remove the retaining ring from the back of the box using a hammer and chisel in the indents to unscrew it. (ring with 3 notches can be seen below)
Once that is removed, use a spanner (or needle nose pliers like I did) to tighten the adjustment plug to snug. Then back it off 3/16" to 1/4" at the perimeter of the disk. (mark the housing to measure this if you have to)


Overcentre Position: For overcentre adjustment, you must first locate the centred position of your gearbox. Count the number of turns lock to lock, then go back half that amount from lock to centre the box.
Once the box is centred, loosen the retaining nut on the top of the box, while holding the adjustment screw with an Allen wrench. Tighten the Allen screw to snug, then tighten the retaining screw. Now rotate the steering shaft using an in-lbs torque wrench and measure the amount of torque required to pass through the centre sweep of the gear box. This reading should not exceed 14 in-lbs at a constant rate (gear box will be stiffer at centre than close to locks).


So that's what I did, cost of this was minimal and was completely worth it. This was also in conjunction with making sure the tie rods were tight, balljoints good, no play in idler/pitman arms etc.

Here's some places where I found info, there's one more I would like to ad but need to find the source.
MonteCarloSS.com Intermediate Shaft info
Monte Carlo Mailing List

Just a disclaimer that I'm not responsible for what YOU do to YOUR truck, this is just an overview, do some reading and confer with other sources to make sure you know what you're doing.

Questions/Comments/Discussion welcome!

UPDATE 14/02/12: Adding information from later in the thread so people don't need to dig too much... Thanks to mc87ss for the info (quotes are paraphrased)

Originally Posted by mc87ss
These shafts make a great upgrade over the old rag joint setup.
Tightens up the steering and gives more clearance along with a cleaner look.
These (referring to the steering shafts he has/the ones shown below) are compressed, cleaned, painted, greased and ready to install.
I spend a lot of time getting them prepped and make sure the finished product is as good as they can be. Mine are separated, cleaned, sanded and painted along with little extras like spreading them so they slide right on, cleaning the bolt threads, greasing them, etc....


There seems to be some conflicting opinions on whether the "D" shaped part of the column needs to be notched or not.
Here is what I discovered about the upper "D" shaped section.

1st there are 2 different types of shafts, I assume it has to do with the year or model.
The set on the right has Cast Ends and the set on the left are Bent Steel. Both sets work exactly the same. The ones with the Cast Ends have a smaller diameter where the rubber isolator is. This could prove beneficial for those with large primary tube headers.



The upper "D" shaft on our cars have a "Top" & "Bottom". These have 2 flats on the sides but the rounded sides are different also. The "Top" is rounded but the "Bottom" has a flat spot for the bolt.



I originally thought the shafts did not require a notch if you align the bolt with the flat spot on the top section. However after a few tests I realized a notch is required. The notch is also a good idea to prevent the coupling from sliding down off the shaft. If you notch the flat side, a smaller grove is required.


Here is how mc87ss notches his steering shafts: (I used a file to make a flat spot on one of mine, it can be done on the truck but is a PITA.

Originally Posted by mc87ss
I have had many questions about the notching of the shaft so i thought some more instruction may be in order.
The notch required for the bolt has to be made on your steering column shaft NOT the Jeep Shaft.
To make things easier i used an extra steering column for the pictures. The area you are seeing is the part of the steering column that comes thru the firewall.
This is what it looks like once you remove your stock shaft.



Slide the Jeep shaft on as shown.



If you look thru the bolt hole you can see where the column shaft sticks out into the opening.



Mark the center of the bolt hole with a marker.





I got carried away with my die grinder so the notch is larger then it needs to be.



Now you can see the bolt hole is clear straight thru.


Bolt installed and shaft locked in from sliding off.



Hopefully this helps.
posts.rewritten_content:
I recently modded my truck's steering system to improve cornering performance, all while keeping costs minimal—around $20 total. To address the intermediate shaft slop caused by a worn rag joint, I sourced a universal joint from a mid-90s Jeep Cherokee, which fit perfectly in my Cutlass. The only modification needed was trimming about 1–2 mm off the steering column end to clear the retaining bolt.

For removal, we unbolted each end of the shaft and removed the steering column (two 15mm bolts), then gently pulled it off. Alternatively, you can drop the steering box for easier access. Ensure the universals are in good condition before purchasing. If necessary, heat the shaft to compress it.

To further tighten the steering, I adjusted the steering box back to its original condition by first removing it from the truck. A ball joint removal tool helps but isn’t essential with proficiency. Carefully drain all fluid and remove the retaining ring using a hammer and chisel or spanner. Set bearing preload by tightening the adjustment plug snugly and backing off 3/16" to 1/4". 

For overcentre position, locate the gearbox's centred position (count lock-to-lock turns and go half that distance). With the top retaining nut loosened and an Allen wrench holding the screw, tighten it snugly. Measure torque using a torque wrench at the centre sweep of the gear box—aim for no more than 14 in-lbs.

Finally, ensure tie rods are tight, ball joints are sound, and there's no play in idler/pitman arms. Resources include MonteCarloSS.com Intermediate Shaft info and the Monte Carlo Mailing List.

Please consult multiple sources before proceeding. I’m not responsible for any modifications you make to your vehicle. Feedback and questions are welcome!

ai_article.rewritten_title: Your HID Questions Answered Here
ai_article.summary: This thread provides a comprehensive guide to High-Intensity Discharge (HID) lights, covering their installation, legality, color temperatures, and more. It includes detailed information on how to install HIDs in various truck models and the proper setup for optimal performance.
seo_outline: Can you install HIDs in your vehicle’s headlights?
What bulbs do I need based on my truck model?
Do I need a relay harness, and why?
How to connect the relay harness
Does the relay harness turn on all 4 headlights with high beams?
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
High-Intensity Discharge (HID) lamps are a type of arc lamp that produce light from an arc between electrodes inside the bulb, filled with gas and metal salts. They require a ballast to start and maintain the arc. HID bulbs are more efficient than halogen bulbs, producing more lumens per watt. However, they need proper housing for optimal performance without causing glare to other drivers.

The simple answer is yes; you can install HIDs in your vehicle's headlights. Several companies provide HID conversions that fit into stock bulb sockets and plug into a ballast. While this method works, the proper way would be to use projector housings specifically designed for HIDs. This setup minimizes light scatter and reduces glare.

The legality of HIDs is gray. Some places consider any HID retrofit illegal, while others allow them if they are in housing designed for HIDs. Government websites do not explicitly make HID kits illegal, so choose a color temperature between 4300K-6000K and ensure the lights don't cause glare.

The specific bulbs needed depend on your truck's model and year. For example, '90-'98 GMT-400 trucks with composite headlights use 9006 lowbeam and 9005 highbeam bulbs. '07+ GMT-900 trucks use H11 lowbeam and 9005 highbeam bulbs. You can find more detailed information on the Sylvania Lighting Guide.

HIDs produce much more light than halogen bulbs, so you don't need to match the wattage of your stock headlights. For instance, a 35w HID produces about twice as many lumens as a 55w halogen bulb. Therefore, 35w HIDs are sufficient for low beams, and 55w high beams would be fine.

HID bulbs can emit light in various colors measured in degrees Kelvin (K). Most offer color temperatures ranging from 3000K to 12000K. The recommended range is 4100-4300K for the whitest, most visible light with maximum lumens and useability.

If you want a white light with a slight blue tint, choose color temperatures between 4300K-6000K. Higher temperatures will produce bluer colors but less visible light. The OEM HIDs are typically in the low-4000K range for optimal visibility and brightness.

You can buy HID bulbs from reputable sellers such as DDM Tuning, VVME, or eBay seller HIDgate. They offer a lifetime warranty, whereas HIDgate and VVME have 1-year warranties.

Some HIDs found on eBay are not true HID bulbs; they are blue-coated halogen bulbs that do not operate like true HIDs.

If your HIDs won't turn on after installation, the inexpensive kits may have reversed polarity. Simply reverse the plug going from your vehicle’s harness into the ballast to resolve this issue.

HIDs take 7-10 seconds to reach full brightness and come on with a quick flash before slowly dimming down and brightening up. This is normal behavior for modern HID bulbs, but retrofit kits might behave differently.

A relay harness pulls power directly from the battery instead of the vehicle’s wiring harness, reducing strain on the factory wiring and headlight switch. It also automatically corrects polarity issues. While not always necessary, it's a good idea to install one if you're using HIDs in GMT-400 OBS trucks or older models.

You will need two HID kits for high and low beams; each kit is needed for the specific bulb type required (low beam or high beam). It would also be wise to have relay harnesses for both kits. The hi-4 relay is a separate modification, but one that should be done when running HIDs.

You do not need an error code eliminator if your vehicle does not give a warning light when a headlight is out. None of the trucks mentioned in this thread require one.

posts.original_html:
There are TONS of repeat questions about HIDs popping up lately, so I though I’d make a sticky to try and sort out a lot of the repetition.

What are HIDs?
High-Intensity Discharge lamps are a type of arc lamp. They have no filament like a traditional halogen bulb. The bulb is filled with both gas and metal salts which produce light from an arc between electrodes inside the bulb. Once ignited, the arc heats the metal salts forming a plasma which increases the intensity of the light produced by the arc. Much light fluorescent lamps, HIDs require the use of a ballast to start and maintain the arc.

Can I put HIDs in my vehicle’s headlights?
The simple answer is yes.

There are several companies that make HID conversions that fit into your stock bulb sockets, plug into a ballast and then plug into your vehicle’s stock wiring. Just know that this is not an optimal setup and can cause dangerous glare for other drivers. Since your halogen housings are not designed for HIDs, you will also have some light scatter.

The proper way to do it would be to get a projector housing designed specifically for HIDs and then retrofit them into your headlight housings. Not everyone has the time, money or skills required to do it this way. With a little attention to the type of headlight housing and aiming of the lamp, you can have HIDs in halogen housings without causing glare for others.

Are HIDs legal?
This is a very gray area. The more you research this the more confusing it can be. Some places say that any and all HID retrofits into a vehicle that didn't roll off the assembly line with them are illegal. Other places say that as long as they're in a housing designed for HIDs they're legal. I have yet to find any government website specifically making the use of HID kits illegal. The best thing you can do is to choose a color temperature that isn't overly blue (4300K-6000K would be best) and make sure that your HIDs aren't causing glare for other drivers.

What bulbs do I need?
That all depends on what year and model truck you drive.

You could try clicking on this amazingly handy link right here: Sylvania Lighting Guide

All '90-'98 GMT-400 trucks with composite headlights use 9006 lowbeam and 9005 highbeam bulbs. '88-'89 trucks with the 4 sealed beam headlights do not take the capsule type bulbs that you need for an HID conversion. You can buy some replacement housings that retain the quad-headlight look, but accept the capsule bulbs or you can update to '90-'98 composite headlights. '88-'98 trucks with the large, single headlights are also sealed beams. You can also get replacement housings that accept capsule bulbs for these.

'99-'07 Classic GMT-800 trucks all use the 9006 lowbeam and 9005 highbeam bulbs as well, with the exception of the Sierra Denali projector headlights which use 9005 bulbs for both lowbeams and highbeams. For fog lights, '99-'02 trucks use 880 bulbs and '03-'07 trucks use 9145 bulbs. The 9145 usually doesn't show up on the selections of HID sellers, in which case, the 9005 is a direct replacement.

'07+ GMT-900 trucks use H11 lowbeam and 9005 highbeam bulbs.

My stock headlights are 55w, so do I need 55w HIDs?
No. HIDs produce light much more efficiently than halogen bulbs. It takes less power to produce more light with HIDs. 35w HIDs, depending on the color temperature, produce a little more than twice the amount of light in lumens as 55w halogen bulbs. 55w HIDs produce approximately another 40% more light than 35w HIDs. 35w HIDs put out more than enough light for low beam headlights making 55w low beams unnecessary. 55w high beams would be fine since they are not the primary lights used to drive with at night.

What are color temperatures?
HIDs can be had in a variety of different colors. The color is measured in degrees Kelvin (K). Most HID sellers offer color temperatures ranging from 3000K to 12000K. There are higher Kelvin temperatures out there, but this is the most common range. 3000K HIDs are going to be very yellow/amber in color and are best left for auxiliary/fog lighting. Stock halogen bulbs are around 3200K. Cars that came factory equipped with HIDs, no matter what the make or model, are all in the 4100 – 4300K range. The low 4000K range will give you the whitest possible light with the most useable lumens and most visibility. Higher temperatures will produce a bluer color with less visible light. An 8000K HID bulb will produce about 20% less visible light than a 4300K HID bulb. There is a reason that the OEM HIDs are in the low-4000K range.



I want a white light with a slight tint of blue. What color temperature should I get?
All HIDs in the 4300 – 12000K range are going to produce a shade of blue. Even 4300K will have a slight tint of blue. I recommend staying below 5000K, but that’s not enough blue color for some. 6000K is the happy medium for those who want some visible blue color, yet still have a white light. Higher than that and the lights start to become very blue and are more likely to attract unwanted attention from law enforcement.

Here are 35w 4500K DDM Tuning HIDs compared with stock halogen highbeams:
Click this bar to view the full image.


These are 35w 5000K HIDgate HIDs compared with stock halogen highbeams:
Click this bar to view the full image.


Notice that even these 2 “white” HID colors are still blue when compared with halogen bulbs.

Where should I buy my HIDs?
I have used 3 different sources to buy HIDs from, all with good results; DDM Tuning, VVME and eBay seller HIDgate. The first 2 sets I bought were from HIDgate. I’ve been using them for a long time now and haven’t had any issues with them. I purchased a set from VVME for a friend because he wanted 4300K and HIDgate doesn’t carry any lower than 5000K. My most recent purchase was from DDM Tuning. I chose DDM because they have 4500K lights and are about $20 cheaper than VVME. HIDgate and VVME both have a 1 year warranty on their lights while DDM Tuning has a lifetime warranty.

I can get some HID/Xenon bulbs on eBay for $10.
These are not true HIDs. They are just blue coated bulbs, often called hyperwhite bulbs, that use buzz-words like “HID” and “Xenon” to lure buyers in. These bulbs do have have ballasts and do not operate like true HIDs. They’re nothing more than blue coated halogen bulbs.

I installed my HIDs, but they won’t turn on. What’s wrong?
These inexpensive HID kits have reversed polarity. The plug going from your vehicle’s harness into the ballast needs to be reversed and your lights should work, then.

My HIDs take a long time to get bright. Is this normal?
Yes, this is normal. Modern OEM HIDs turn on almost instantly, but these retrofit kits will take a good 7-10 seconds to reach full brightness. They come on with a quick, bright flash. They then dim down and then slowly become brighter until they are fully warmed up to their operating temperature.

What is a relay harness?
A relay harness (called a dual in/dual out harness on the DDM Tuning site) pulls the power for the HIDs directly from the battery instead of from the vehicle’s wiring harness. Even though HIDs require less power to run than halogens, they do require a considerable amount of power when they are first ignited. A vehicle’s wiring is often not up to the task of handling the power requirements of that initial ignition, which can lead to misfires.

A common symptom is that only one HID will come on. The wiring has enough to handle the ignition of one light, but not both. Usually, the other HID can be ignited by turning the headlights off and then back on again quickly.

Another common symptom is the flickering of the headlights when they’re on. The power flow is not constant enough to keep them steady.

The relay harness will also automatically correct the polarity so you don’t have to worry about which way your ballasts are plugged in.

Do I need a relay harness?
It never hurts to have one. It’s cheap piece of mind. For all GMT-400 OBS trucks and older, I recommend one without question. I have installed HIDs in a ’94 and a ’91 without a harness and didn’t have any issues. I’ve installed HIDs in a ’97 and a ’98 and did have misfires in both. A relay harness on both trucks solved those problems. Even though some trucks may not seem to need one, it would still be best to install one to relieve the strain from the factory wiring and headlight switch.

The newer trucks already have relays on their headlight systems and don’t really need them, though I’m not sure when this started. I know some GMT-800 NBS trucks have them, but I believe the early GMT-800s don’t.

How do I connect the relay harness?
Most pre-made relay harnesses should have a red positive and black ground ring connector, 2 male headlight connectors and 1 female headlight connector. The harness should look something like this...


Connect the red positive to your battery's positive terminal.
Connect the black negative to a good ground on the truck.
The 2 male headlight connectors will connect to the ballasts.
The 1 female headlight connector will connect to the truck's harness. It doesn't matter which side (driver or passenger) you connect it to, it's the switched power for the harness and will work with either one.

You'll end up with a couple of unused plugs hanging around, but that's normal. As long as you have all of the relay harness connections properly hooked up, you should be good to go.

Does the relay harness turn on all 4 headlight with my high beams?
No. The hi-4 relay is a separate modification, but one that should be done when running HIDs.

What do I need for HID high and low beams?
You’ll need 2 HID kits to have HID highs and lows. You’ll need the kit for your low beam bulbs and a separate kit for your high beam bulbs. It would also be a good idea to have a relay harness for each HID kit as well.

Do I need an error code eliminator?
No. The error code eliminator is for vehicles that give a warning light when a headlight is out. None of our trucks have this.

I’m ordering from DDM Tuning, do I need the Raptor kit or the Slim kit?
Both the Raptor and the slim kits are functionally identical. There is no operational advantage to buying the slim kit. The only difference is in packaging. The slim kit is more intended for vehicles with cramped engine bays that don’t have a lot of room for mounting the ballasts. Space isn’t a big issue for fullsize GM trucks, so there’s no need in the extra expense of the slims.



I'm sure there are some questions that I didn't think of here. If it's not here, just ask.

ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This thread documents an ambitious project to restore a 1978 Nomad travel trailer by user '88GMCtruck'. The trailer, acquired for $250, is in good exterior condition but requires significant interior work due to water damage and subfloor issues.

Trailer condition before restoration:
- Good exterior with minor cleaning required
- Excellent interior fabric and fixtures, with functional kitchen appliances and a full bath
- Subfloor made of chipboard prone to moisture damage; roof needs sealing
- Some partial wall and paneling replacements needed due to water damage

Restoration progress updates include:
- Replaced trailer subfloor and roofing materials
- Installed new tires and inspected/replaced wheel bearings and brakes
- Cleaned, sanitized interior, including fridge and water tank
- Repaired exterior lighting; considering LED upgrades in the future
- Completed significant flooring work with additional bracing and insulation added
- Plans to install a weight-distributing hitch for better towing performance

posts.original_html:
Well, I'm up to another project yet again.

Here we have my newest driveway edition: a 1978 Nomad 16' travel trailer. It has a full bath, full kitchen, dinette, couch/bed, and bunk. It has a very nice and open floorplan.
Click this bar to view the full image.

Click this bar to view the full image.


I picked this up just outside of town for a whopping $250. It's been unlicenced/unused since 2003.

The good: It's in good shape outside, just needs a good pressure washing. Inside, all the fabric, fixtures, counters, appliances etc are in great condition. Everything works great.

The bad: Outside, the lights don't all work yet, but that should just be a cleaning/ground issue. the tires look to be original, as they are GoodYear 7.75-15ST tires and have LARGE cracks all over. Inside is going to take the most effort. The subfloor is toast. Stupid trailer manufacturer decided to use chip board for a floor, that crumbles with any moisture. The roof is solid, but part of the paneling inside needs replaced. One small portion of wall needs replaced as well due to some water damage. The roof obviously needs sealed.

So yeah. It's a project. The goal is to have a nice, reliable camper that I can hitch up the truck to and just take off for the weekend. I'll be towing this with the 88 primarily. So, here is the list of items that will be done to the truck and trailer

Truck:
- re-install brake controller
- buy weight distributing hitch
- buy towing mirrors
- install relay and wiring for trailer lights. I've had too many dash light switches burn out on me
- possibly install my 3/4ton springs, or re-install my helper bags with some quick disconnect
- re-gear truck to 4.56s or 4.88s. This one has been in the works awhile now anyway

Trailer:
- replace subfloor, roof skin and partial wall skin
- replace tires and inspect/replace wheel bearings and brakes
- re-seal roof and windows
- fix exterior lighting, possibly replace with LED at some point
- obvious clean and sanitize insides, fridge and water tank
- thinking about re-painting the sides something a little more modern, maybe to match the truck

So anyway, I'll be updating this as I go along, with my budget trailer resto.
posts.rewritten_content:

Pros:
- Good exterior condition; needs pressure washing
- Excellent interior condition: all fabrics, fixtures, counters, and appliances work

Cons:
- Exterior lights need cleaning or grounding
- Original tires have large cracks, likely original
- Subfloor is damaged due to moisture
- Some roof paneling and a section of wall require replacement
- Roof needs sealing
- Interior requires thorough cleaning and sanitization

Towing truck (1988):
- Reinstall brake controller
- Install weight distributing hitch and towing mirrors
- Add relay and wiring for trailer lights
- Consider installing 3/4-ton springs or re-installing helper bags with quick disconnect
- Gear the truck to either 4.56s or 4.88s

Trailer work:
- Replace subfloor, roof skin, and part of the wall
- Replace tires and inspect/replacing wheel bearings and brakes
- Re-seal roof and windows
- Fix exterior lighting; possibly replace with LED later
- Clean and sanitize inside, including fridge and water tank
- Consider repainting the sides for a more modern look

I'll update this as I progress with my budget trailer restoration.

I redid an '84 Scotty a couple of years back before I got mad at it and sold it and bought a new Jayco 32 BHDS. I tow it with my '99 1500 ECSB Z71. I bought a set of 3/4 springs for it. It helped it quite a bit while towing.

ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This thread discusses the experiences of owners with General Motors' 96-99 7.4L (Vortec 454) engines, focusing on their potential, modifications, and performance.

General Motors introduced the Vortec 454 in the late 1990s as a powerful alternative to smaller V8 engines. However, many owners have noted that these engines are often restricted by various components such as the intake manifold and exhaust system (Post ID: 2657).

Several mods have been popular among owners. These include performance exhaust systems like Banks Powerpack or Flowmaster setups (Post ID: 2661). Some enthusiasts also recommend a cam swap, especially using a ZZ502 camshaft (Post ID: 2664), to unlock more potential from the engine.

Tuning plays a crucial role in enhancing performance. A Wait4Me tune has been widely recommended as it significantly improves midrange and WOT power (Post ID: 2671). However, some owners noted that stock PCM tunes can also provide decent performance, especially with higher octane fuel (Post ID: 3098).

Owners have shared their experiences regarding towing efficiency. Those who tow often find that 454-equipped trucks can offer better performance when tuned properly for towing applications (Post ID: 2670).

the Vortec big blocks run a very different injection system than the small blocks do. The bigblock injection is by far more desirable because it uses conventional fuel injectors which can be replaced with larger sizes without changing the intake manifold.

IIRC the 454 Vortec uses 24 lb/hr LT1 fuel injectors. It is rated at 290 hp and 410 lb/ft torque.

The cylinder heads are very restrictive to power production. I have seen Vortec 454's dyno at 217 hp at the rear wheels in a 1 ton truck, torque was over 320 lb ft at the wheels.

headwork along with a cam can really wake these 454's up. They are a step up from the TBI 454's which make their peak torque at 1800 rpm. They came in 230 hp 385 lb/ft and 255hp 405 lb/ft flavours.

A nice set of aluminum 502 heads woiuld work nicely in tehse trucks, or drop in 502 shortblock.

I have a Wait4Me tune. Overall good. It REALLY wakes up with 93 octane. I think he is still pretty conservative with 87 octane. But still a world difference over stock. I suspect WOT power is similar on 87 octane, but much improved in the midrange and 93 octane (there is 2 octane maps, so it can react with both if the octane is pumped up)

Best $75 you will spend.

If you have a Wait4Me tune, and haven't filled up with 93, go to some 0-60 times and then fill up with 93 (try to keep vehicle weight similar and octane pure as you can) and you will see some improvments. ai_article.rewritten_title: Recalls & Engine Knock Information
ai_article.summary: This thread discusses engine knock issues in certain Chevrolet and GMC models, as well as recalls for fuel system and body door hinge assemblies. General Motors has addressed the engine knock by providing a technical service bulletin (TSB) recommending carbon cleaning.
seo_outline: General Motors' Response to Engine Knocks
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
In 2002, General Motors recalled nearly 525,254 vehicles including the 2000 Chevrolet Suburban, Tahoe, Silverado, GMC Yukon/Yukon XL, and Sierra due to airbag problems. Additionally, in 2003, several models were recalled for fuel system and body door hinge issues.

Engine knock at start-up has been reported by owners of certain GM vehicles from 1999 to 2002. General Motors addressed this concern with a technical service bulletin (TSB) explaining that the noise is due to carbon build-up on pistons. The manufacturer states that it does not warrant a recall or repair, but dealers will offer free de-carbonization services under warranty.

For the fuel and door hinge issues in 2003 models, the recalls involve Chevrolet Suburban, Tahoe, Yukon/Yukon XL, and GMC Sierra and Yukon. Dealers will inspect and correct any issues identified during vehicle checks.

posts.original_html:
I just read this and thought some of you may be interested in reading it as well:

From Pages 90-91 of the March/April '03 issue of TruckTrend

We've finally gotten an answer on the cold-start piston knock involving 4.8, 5.3 and 6.0-liter V8's in '99 to '02 GM cars and trucks. General Motors has previously released a Technical Service Bulletin explaining the condition that occurs after approximately 12,000 miles and a normal accumulation of carbon above the top piston ring.

I spoke with Sam Winegarden, GM program manager and chief engineer for small- and big-block engines. Sam explains that following extensive testing, General Motors is confident the start-up noise will have no adverse effect on performance or durability of the engines involved.

As opposed to the larger pistons of earlier design engines, today's technical refinement requires the use of smaller pistons to reduce weight and reciprocating mass in order to aid in efficiency and durability. This reduction in size also reduces the stability of the piston in the cylinder bore, which can promote piston noise.

Preliminary testing on these engines showed no sign of a problem, but, as in many other situations, the symptoms came to the surface after the vehicles were subject to normal driving conditions.

The manufacturer's stand on the issue is that it doesn't warrant a service bulletin or recall promoting a repair. We were also assured the problem has been corrected on the '03-model line with a piston-design modification along with the addition of a polymer coating.

My response was from the viewpoint of a consumer who purchased a brand-new vehicle that developed a notable engine knock before the first major service. The complaint was not only about the annoyance of the condition, but also the effect on resale and depreciation.

The answer was that General Motors would be dealing with the consumer on a case-by-case basis, and complaints have been resolved by means of warranty extension and parts replacement.

The owners of involved vehicles exhibiting the cold-start piston knock should have the service manager of the GM dealership, which has been evaluating the noise, contact the manufacturer's zone representative. Hopefully you can come to satisfactory terms.

posts.rewritten_content:
I am a new Service Manager at an unnamed Chevrolet dealership and I may be able to provide some insight based on the posts here. 

1. There has been no engine failure due to the piston issue reported; however, there was a post about a connecting rod failure—different situation and noise.

2. A GM TSB addresses an "torn" O-ring at the oil pump pickup causing oil aeration. This is an assembly problem that should have been noticed initially.

3. The noise you’re experiencing is due to carbon buildup on the pistons, which can be removed ("decarbonized"), but it returns over time.

Decarbonizing effectively:
1. Remove spark plugs.
2. Purchase "top engine clean" from your local dealer (non-California).
3. Pour into each cylinder and let sit overnight.
4. Turn engine 180 degrees and pour more "top engine clean."
5. Let it sit overnight again.
6. Re-install spark plugs, start the engine; expect smoke and foul smell.
7. Once stopped smoking, change oil.

A GM TSB listed part numbers for updated pistons, which I replaced with Diamond forged ones on my 2003 model without issues.

Thank you for your understanding!

You can see the full range of these pics at: www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges01.jpg through hinges23.jpg, just keep changing the numbers to see the progress. It was a quick-n-dirty pictorial so just remember, the advice is worth what you paid for it.

One FINAL NOTE that is important. If you've got power windows, DO NOT, DO NOT, DO NOT close the door while the harnesses are disconnected. If the connectors are just hanging out in the door jamb, you will almost surely bust the crap out of them when the door closes!

*Added 9/22/10 - if you want to see what letting them get really bad does, check out: www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges25.jpg, www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges26.jpg, www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges27.jpg ! NASTY...

*Added 9/22/10 - if you let the sagging door condition go too long, it will "egg out" the hole in the top hinge half on the door side. This means once you do bushings and pins, it will still sag and have slop, and wear out too soon. The only "official" fix for this is to replace the hinge, which is a MAJOR pain, and the hinges are expensive. A hack fix which actually works long-term is to go ahead and replace everything, but ditch the upper retainer for that top pin. Scrape away the paint from the hinge area immediately surrounding the pin and also an area lower on the same hinge to attach the welder ground to. Jack the door up with a block of wood from the rear so it pushes the slack in the hole forwards toward the front of the truck. Stitch just a LITTLE BIT of weld to fill up the hole and retain the pin. Don't put too much because if you ever need to remove the door later (like to replace from a crash) you have very little room to work to cut the weld for removing the pin. THIS FIX WORKS.

Richard
posts.rewritten_content:
I prefer using an engine hoist method for installing hinges, as it is safer and more efficient. A thick towel wrapped around the door frame with a strap secured by the hoist works well. This is a one-man job. For detailed step-by-step images, see www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges01.jpg through hinges23.jpg.

For those with slightly lower trucks, propping the door open with a milk crate can simplify the process, but be cautious to avoid scratches.

If you have power windows, do not close the door while disconnecting harnesses. This could damage the window connectors.

An important note: Excessive sagging can "egg out" the top hinge hole, leading to premature wear and potential issues even after bushings and pins are installed. In such cases, replacing the entire hinge is necessary but difficult. A practical workaround is to remove the upper retainer, clean the hinge area, and perform a spot weld to fill the hole without restricting future removal of the door.

This fix ensures long-term reliability.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Chevy Lean - Diagnosing and Fixing Left Front Vehicle Sits Low
ai_article.summary: This article covers the symptoms of a vehicle with an uneven front, detailing the diagnostic steps and potential solutions. It includes advice on measuring ride height, verifying springs, and installing upper insulators.
seo_outline: Symptom Description: Left front of vehicle sits low
Diagnosis Steps: Measure trim height, check spring heights, install insulator if needed
Potential Solutions: Installing upper insulators, other possible fixes like swaybars
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This article covers the symptoms of a vehicle with an uneven front. Specifically, the left front of the vehicle sits lower than the right side. The following steps are recommended to diagnose and potentially fix this issue:

- **Measure Trim Height**: It is important to verify that the trim height difference between the sides does not exceed 0.5 inches.
- **Check Front Springs**: Ensure both front springs are of the correct production model. Measure their standing heights to ensure they are equal.
- **Install Upper Insulator (P/N 15756770)**: If the above checks do not resolve the issue, install a single upper insulator in the lower control arm spring pocket at a time. Maximum two per spring pocket may be used.

Other potential solutions include checking and adjusting steering alignment and headlight aim if ride height was changed. Additionally, if the vehicle is out of warranty, collision repair shops can sometimes provide this service for around $150.

evidence.article_excerpt: Measure front trim height keeping in mind that the trim height tolerance is .5" difference side to side.
Verify that the vehicle is equipped with the correct production front springs. You should measure the standing height of both front springs to ensure that they are equal height.

Install a front spring upper insulator, P/N 15756770 in the lower control arm spring pocket. Install 1 insulator at a time and measure the change between installations. A maximum of 2 insulators per spring pocket may be used.
The steering alignment and headlight aim must be checked if the vehicle ride height was changed.

seo_outline: Introduction to recalling vehicles and why it’s important
How to use VIN to check for recalls
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
Checking if your vehicle has an outstanding recall is a straightforward process. Members in this thread provide assistance by running their vehicle's VIN through General Motors (GM) systems at work or with other professionals who have access to such data. However, it’s important to note that the system may not have records for vehicles older than 10 years.

TRITON20 initially offered to check VINS and provide recall information but stated he was no longer able to do so due to restrictions at work. Others in the thread mentioned continuing this tradition by working at dealerships, suggesting you can still post your VIN here for others to check if they have access to these systems.

According to TRITON20, running a vehicle's VIN through GM’s system allows checking for outstanding recalls but does not provide information on other service history such as damage from accidents or floods. For instance, he explained that the recall related to tailgate cable replacement was completed in June 2005 under recall number 04007.

Some members posted their VINS and received recall confirmations or negative results. TRITON20 also mentioned that vehicles older than 92-93 might not be viewable due to them being deleted from GM’s data base.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Rear End Ratio Codes and Their Meanings
ai_article.summary: This thread provides a list of RPO codes for different rear end ratios in Chevrolet trucks, including their meanings and locations. Users discuss the presence of these codes in their vehicles.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
The thread provides a list of RPO codes for different rear end ratios in Chevrolet trucks. The codes include GQ1, GT4, GT5, GU4, GU5, GU6, and G80. These codes can be found on the bottom of a sticker inside the glovebox.

These are some of the codes:
- **GQ1**: AXLE REAR, STD RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GT4**: AXLE REAR, 3.73 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GT5**: AXLE REAR, 4.10 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GU4**: AXLE REAR, 3.08 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GU5**: AXLE REAR, 3.23 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **GU6**: AXLE REAR, 3.42 RATIO (Post ID: 2755)
- **G80**: AXLE REAR, LIMITED SLIP (POSITRACTION) (Post ID: 2755)

Users also discuss the presence of a code for a 4.56 ratio in military trucks (Post ID: 2763).

Regarding the G80 code, users are unsure if it indicates a gear ratio or a locking differential function (Post IDs: 2759, 2761, 2762, 2764, 2765, 2766). Brendan explains that G80 is for the limited slip, not the ratio (Post ID: 2764).

Another user mentions that G80 works well in their vehicle but others report issues with it locking inconsistently (Post IDs: 2769, 2771, 2773, 2775).

threads.title: Common Lift/Tire Combo's for OBS/NBS Trucks & SUVs

ai_article.rewritten_title: Common Lift/Tire Combinations for OBS/NBS Trucks & SUVs
ai_article.summary: This article compiles common lift/tire combinations for Obsidian (OBS) and New Body Structure (NBS) trucks and SUVs, ranging from stock height to a total of 9 inches of lift. It provides guidance on tire sizes suitable for different lifts and offers insights into potential clearance issues.
seo_outline: Common Lift/Tire Combinations for OBS Trucks/SUVs
Common Lift/Tire Combinations for NBS Trucks/SUVs
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
These are only common lift/tire combinations that seem to work well together. Some setups may rub in off-highway situations, but most allow for clearance. Any wheel that is 'not recommended' for that particular height can be run, but is not advisable.

### Common Lift/Tire Combinations for OBS Trucks/SUVs (88-98, 92-99)

#### Stock Height
- 285/75R16 & 32/11.5R15 on Stock wheels or 16x8/15x8 (possible torsion bar crank); 16x10/15x10 not recommended
- 305/70R16 & 33/12.5R15 on Stock wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and light trimming); 16x10/15x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares)

#### 3" Suspension Lift or Body Lift
- 305/70R16 & 33/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8; 16x10/15x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming)
- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares); 16x10/15x10 not recommended

#### 4" Suspension Lift
- 305/70R16 & 33/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8; 16x10/15x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming)
- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10/15x10 (cutout flares)

#### 6" Total Lift (3" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift or 6" Suspension Lift)
- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8; 16x10/15x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming) 
- 36/12.5R16 & 36/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10/15x10 not recommended

#### 7" Total Lift (4" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift)
- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels, 16x8/15x8, or 16x10/15x10
- 36/12.5R16 & 36/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and light trimming); 16x10/15x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares)

#### 9" Total Lift (6" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift)
- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels, 16x8/15x8, or 16x10/15x10
- 36/12.5R16 & 36/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels, 16x8/15x8, or 16x10/15x10
- 38/15.5R16 & 38/15.5R15 on 16x10/15x10 (torsion bar crank and light trimming)

### Common Lift/Tire Combinations for NBS Trucks/SUVs (99-03, 00-03)

#### Stock Height
- 285/75R16 on Stock wheels or 16x8 (possible torsion bar crank); 16x10 not recommended
- 305/70R16 on Stock wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and light trimming); 16x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares)

#### 3" Suspenion Lift or Body Lift
- 305/70R16 and under on Stock Wheels or 16x8; 16x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares); 16x10 not recommended

#### 4" Suspension Lift
- 305/70R16 and under on Stock Wheels or 16x8; 16x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10 (cutout flares)

#### 6" Total Lift (3" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift or 6" Suspension Lift)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8; 16x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming) 
- 36/12.5R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10 not recommended

#### 7" Total Lift (4" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels, 16x8, or 16x10 
- 36/12.5R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and light trimming); 16x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares)

#### 9" Total Lift (6" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels, 16x8, or 16x10 
- 36/12.5R16 on Stock Wheels, 16x8, or 16x10 
- 38/15.5R16 on 16x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming)

*Note: Thanks to those who double-checked everything and added more info.

- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares); 16x10/15x10 not recommended

4" Suspension Lift
- 305/70R16 & 33/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8; 16x10/15x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming)

- 36/12.5R16 & 36/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10/15x10 not recommended

- 36/12.5R16 & 36/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels or 16x8/15x8 (torsion bar crank and light trimming); 16x10/15x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares)

- 315/75R16 & 35/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels, 16x8/15x8, or 16x10/15x10
- 36/12.5R16 & 36/12.5R15 on Stock Wheels, 16x8/15x8, or 16x10/15x10

Stock height

- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10 (cutout flares)

6" Total Lift (3" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift or 6" Suspension Lift)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8; 16x10 (possible torsion bar crank and light trimming)
- 36/12.5R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming); 16x10 not recommended

7" Total Lift (4" Suspension Lift + 3" Body Lift)
- 315/75R16 on Stock Wheels, 16x8, or 16x10
- 36/12.5R16 on Stock Wheels or 16x8 (torsion bar crank and light trimming); 16x10 (torsion bar crank and heavy trimming, or cutout flares)

ai_article.rewritten_title: Best Bagging Setup for Trucks
ai_article.summary: This thread discusses various setups for bagging trucks, including rear kits, compressors, front ends, and budgets. Users share their experiences and recommendations.
seo_outline: Rear Bagging Kits: KP Components Bolt-on 4-Link with Cantilever Attachment
Compressors: Air Commander by Airlift Company
Bags for the Rear: Airlift 2b7 1/2" Port Bags
Front End Setup: Air Ride Coolride Kit with Slam Specialties RS-72 Bags and Bilstein Shocks
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
When considering bagging a truck, the community recommends several key components that can significantly enhance your vehicle's performance and comfort. Here are some top setups based on user recommendations.

### Rear Bagging Kits
Many users recommend the **KP Components Bolt-on 4-Link with Cantilever Attachment** as it offers great ride quality and a moderate difficulty level for installation, estimated at around 6 out of 10 due to grinding rivets. ([Post ID: 3694], [Post ID: 3708])

### Compressors
For the compressor setup, the **Air Commander** from Airlift Company is popular. It consists of a York 209 compressor that comes with all necessary components such as mounting brackets, clutch, pressure switch, fittings, airline, check valve, and water/oil trap. The installation difficulty is about 4 out of 10. ([Post ID: 3694])

### Rear Bags
Airlift's **2b7 1/2" Port Bags** are favored for their great performance with the KP kit. ([Post ID: 3694])

### Valves
**SMC 3/8” Quick Response Valves** have been highly recommended by users due to their quick responsiveness and ease of use. ([Post ID: 3694])

### Air Tanks
An **Airlift 8.5 Gallon Tank** is suitable for most setups, especially when mounted under the bed or near the roll pan to avoid hanging below. ([Post ID: 3694], [Post ID: 3708])

### Front End Setup
For the front end, the **Air Ride Coolride Kit** with **Slam Specialties RS-72 Bags** and homemade shock mounts using Bilstein shocks is suggested for a comfortable ride. The installation difficulty is around 5 out of 10. ([Post ID: 3694])
