posts.original_html:
If everyone could, give your opinion on different bag setups. I've noticed a ton of bag questions, many of which are the exact same. If a mod could sticky this, it would be great.


My advice:

For the rear, the KP Components bolt on 4 link with cantilever attachment rides great. I, as well as many others, love this kit. The difficulty of the install was prolly a 6 out of 10, due to grinding a ton of rivits. You basically need regular hand tools, such as a grinder, drill with a step bit,a jack, jackstands, socket wrenches, box end wrenches, and a BFH. www.kpcomponents.com

For compressors, I am running the Air Commander, which consists of a York 209 compressor, which was used on older fords for the A/C. The kit comes with everything to hook the compressor up:mounting brackets, clutch, pressure switch, fittings, airline, check valve, water/oil trap, etc. The install was very straight forward, with a difficulty of about 4 out of 10. I had to modify my mounting brackets a little to fit, but no biggie. The compressor is made by Airlift. www.airliftcompany.com

For bags on the back I am running the Airlift 2b7 1/2" port bags. They feel great on the KP kit.

For valves, I am having great luck with (8) 3/8" smc valves. They are very quick.

For a tank, I am using the Airlift 8.5 gallon, which mounts under my bed, and doesnt hang below the rollpan. I have enough room to mount 2 under the bed on my obs.

For the front end, I recommend the Air Ride coolride setup, which consists of the tubular uca's and lca's to correct balljoing angles. It also has the cups, bolt on brackets for shocks, the shocks, and bags. I do not own the kit, but hopefully I will one day. I'd say the difficulty of this is about a 5 out of 10, using basic hand tools.

Up front, I am using cups from www.innovativeairsuspension.com Slam Specialties RS-72 bags, and homemade shock mounts with bilstein shocks. The front end rides very nice with this setup. I also have 2" spindles. I have not notched the frame for tierods, so I'm 1.5" from laying out up front.

Everyone add what you think is appropriate.
posts.rewritten_content:
If possible, share your experiences and recommendations on different bag setups. A sticky thread by a moderator would be great.

For the rear end, the KP Components bolt-on 4-link with cantilever attachment performs exceptionally well. The installation difficulty rates around a 6 out of 10 due to extensive rivet grinding. Regular hand tools are required, including a grinder, drill with step bit, jack, jackstands, socket wrenches, box-end wrenches, and a BFH.

For compressors, I use the Air Commander kit from Airlift, featuring a York 209 compressor. The package includes mounting brackets, clutch, pressure switch, fittings, airline, check valve, water/oil trap, etc. Installation is straightforward with a difficulty level of about 4 out of 10. Minor modifications to the mounting brackets were necessary.

For rear bags, I use Airlift 2B7 1/2" port bags, which complement the KP kit well. For valves, (8) 3/8" SMC valves provide excellent performance and quick response.

For a tank, an Airlift 8.5-gallon model mounts under the bed without hanging below the roll pan. Room allows for mounting two tanks beneath the bed on my OBS.

In the front end, I recommend the Air Ride Coolride setup with tubular UCA's and LCA’s to correct ball joint angles. The kit includes cups, bolt-on brackets for shocks, shocks, and bags. Installation difficulty is approximately 5 out of 10 using basic hand tools. For now, I use Innovative Air Suspension cups, Slam Specialties RS-72 bags, homemade shock mounts with Bilstein shocks, and 2-inch spindles. Frame notching for tie rods has been avoided, leaving me 1.5 inches from laying out the frame.

Share your thoughts!

posts.rewritten_content:
My setup includes KP Components 6-link lift, which provides twice the lift and an improved ride, mounting easily to the leaf spring hanger locations. I use SMC 1/2" valves with mufflers on the dumps, significantly reducing noise and improving control.

For air management, I have an Air Commander engine-driven compressor, as it is the most efficient option for my needs. Typically, my fill lasts between 150-185 seconds, taking less than 30 seconds to complete. This setup is quieter and doesn't drain the battery, making it a cost-effective alternative compared to using two Viair compressors or an Optima battery.

I use the Dakota Digital ARC-1004 gauge, which offers both digital readouts and switch functionality on the gauge itself. Remote controls are highly recommended as they allow operation even when the truck is off. Additionally, I recommend installing a Schroeder valve on the air tanks for backup in case of compressor failure or if starting the truck proves difficult.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Tips for Lowering Your Truck’s Static Height
ai_article.summary: This thread provides insights from a truck owner who went through various modifications to lower his 96 Chevy extended cab by 5/8 of an inch. The discussion covers necessary components, potential issues, and recommendations.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This post shares valuable insights from a truck owner who lowered his 96 Chevy extended cab by 5/8 of an inch. Starting with a 3/4 drop, he eventually opted for a more aggressive 5/8 drop to improve the stance and ride quality. Here are some key points to consider:

- **Starting Equipment**: The author initially used 3-inch coils and 2-inch hangers but found them problematic. He recommends using 3" coils and 2" spindles in the front, with a flip kit and shackles in the back.

- **Front Suspension Issues**: For lower drops than 4 inches (such as a 5/8 drop), cutting a notch in the frame for tie rod ends is necessary to avoid scraping. The author mentions that his truck has plenty of travel in the frame notch, allowing him to lay down on 22-inch wheels easily.

- **Sway Bar Considerations**: Using the stock sway bar can lead to issues with fit and function. The author suggests removing it temporarily but acknowledges its importance for stability. He recommends redesigning the swaybar mounts or using shorter endlinks if DJM spindles are used.

- **Notch Modifications**: The author opted for a 8-inch notch from Suicidedoors.com, which he claims provides plenty of travel for his truck.

- **Customization and Adjustments**: Proper alignment is crucial after installing new components. The author mentions issues with the swaybar fit due to the DJM spindles but found that redrilling the mounts resolved the problem.

- **Wheels and Tires**: For optimal performance, he suggests using 45 or 50 series tires on roads with poor conditions.

posts.original_html:
Long post ahead. I got a PM and see many threads addressing questions about how to go about static drops and how they work in real life, so I thought I would make a post putting my .02 cents in, having driven a 96 chevy extended cab slammed 5/8 every day for 8 months now, day in and day out.

I'm going to give you all some good advice, because I have learned a lot working on my truck, doing all the work myself, and having to rely on it for sole transportation (which can be tricky at times like now, when its down most of the time for a full custom paint job ) . Anyway, as far as the suspension goes, I was/am in the same boat as you. I started with a 3/4 drop, and while it was cool and very streetable, I didn't like the rake too much. I wanted bags, couldn't afford it at the time. The reason I went with the 5/8 was because I already had the 3" coils and 2" hangers. That was mistake #1. Hangers. They are a total pain. You have to pull the bed to put them on and the rivets on the driver's side are blocked by the gas tank. So, I went my merry way to the local hot rod shop and picked up a 6" flip kit and 2" lower control arms. Mistake #2. LCAs + coils = alignment issues. I'm going to swap them out for spindles, and I will be able to align it all back to spec, and they wont rub the inner lip of my $600 apiece wheels like they do now Now, a 4/6 is a very streetable drop. The only real thing you have to cut is the frame for the bolt in notch. Sure, a 4/6 is cool.. but you want to go that extra mile right? I did. So, when you take the plunge and go 5/8 ( you know you want to) you'll want to use 3" coils and 2" spindles in the front, and a flipkit and shackles in the back. You could think that you'll be okay on the bolt in notch like I did, but you'll hate it instantly. There's no travel. So, knowing that I will want bags later, i went ahead and cut the bed out and welded in a monster notch from Suicidedoors.com . But, if you dont want the big hole and dont care about laying out all the way, get the same notch i did ( the 8" one ) and just trim it down to fit under the bed floor. I have plenty of travel in my notch, I can lay frame on 22s easy. Now, for the front, anything lower than 4" and you have to cut a notch in the frame for your tie rod ends. If those break youre screwed. You'll also notice your swaybar doesnt fit. Dont chunk it - I ran without it for a while and yes, it does make a big difference in these big trucks. What you'll need is some shorter endlinks. However, if you use DJM lca's, you'll notice that their brilliant engineering department designed them so that the swaybar is at some goofy angle and you end up busting out your bushings. Solution = redrill and tap the swaybar mounts on the frame. Also, dont forget your carrier bearing shim. Nothing is worse than taking off from a stop and getting that extra vibration jiggling your hot, expensive Starbucks all over your dash. If you go 5" in the front, and even with a wheel and tire combo that equals 27" in overall diameter like my 20s with 255/35ZR20 tires, you'll need to cut out or better yet modify your inner fenders in the front, cause rubbing them and bumping them sucks. And for peace of mind, even though my billet Intro wheels tuck perfectly, I rolled all 4 of my fender lips - no worries. And if your roads even slightly suck like they do here, you'll want a slightly larger profile tire, like a 45 or 50 series, something in there. Good luck, and remember - No fat chicks, the truck will scrape!

Cody
posts.rewritten_content:
I recently drove a 1996 Chevy Extended Cab Slam 5/8 for 8 months daily and can share valuable insights on static drops. While a 3/4 drop is streetable, I found the rake unsatisfactory and opted for a 5/8 drop due to existing 3" coils and 2" hangers, which turned out to be a mistake. The hangers required a bed pull, and driver-side rivets were blocked by the gas tank.

Mistake #2: I installed 6" flip kits with lower control arms (LCAs). This led to alignment issues. Now, swapping for spindles will correct this, preventing wheel rub.

A 4/6 drop is streetable but lacking in travel. For a full 5/8 drop, use 3" coils and 2" spindles in the front with a flip kit and shackles in the rear. Cutting a frame notch for tie rod ends or swaybar compatibility is necessary; redrill swaybar mounts if using DJM LCAs to avoid bushing damage.

Ensure a carrier bearing shim to eliminate vibration, especially when starting. For 27" overall diameter tires like mine, modify inner fenders in the front to prevent rubbing and ensure fender lips are rolled for peace of mind.

In areas with poor roads, opt for slightly larger profile tires (45-50 series) for comfort. Remember, no fat chicks—this truck will scrape!

posts.rewritten_content:
For a 2-inch lift, the lower control arm (LCA) pushes the tie rod mount upward on the spindles. A 2-inch drop spindle maintains the stock tie rod mount. With a 6.5-inch front drop, there was no tie rod scraping. Now, using a 5.5-inch daily drop also prevents scraping.

Fender wells need to be moved outward to avoid contact. I encountered them frequently throughout the day.

For a 6-inch drop shock absorber extenders are essential; differential support is crucial for extended cab V8s. Use Belltech Adjustable Shackles for better alignment and clearance. Hangers can cause issues with clearance.

A Y-pipe should be raised if you have more than a 4-inch drop. In the rear, dump the exhaust before the axle for drops of 7 inches or greater.

A 4- to 7-inch drop is generally advisable without cutting into components. My ordered low/static components will be removed.

ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This thread provides a comprehensive guide on finding and installing YORK compressors in various vehicles. It covers sourcing information, mounting brackets, clutches, plumbing setup, and additional maintenance tips.

Where to Find York Compressors:
- Quite a bit of Pre 1984 Volvo's had a York 210. This is your best bet. [Post ID: 3834]
- Other Cars include (stole this list from my roommate who posted it on SSM):
    - 1963-1968 AMERICAN MOTORS AMBASSADOR
    - 1964-1968 AMERICAN MOTORS AMERICAN
    - 1963-1966 AMERICAN MOTORS CLASSIC
    - [Many more car models listed here] [Post ID: 3834]

Mounting Brackets and Clutches:
- You need to mount this thing somehow. Decide weather you want to run it off your alternator, in your serpentine belt rotation, or anywhere else. Onboard Air and Air Ride Technologies sell brackets for popular applications. [Post ID: 3835]
- If you want to run your york in your serpentine belt rotation, you will need a **serpentine clutch**. I have a V-belt clutch on my york, because i run a **Kilby Combo Pully**.[Post ID: 3835]

Plumbing Setup:
- You need to get some way of converting the rotolock thread flanges to NPT so you can run standard fittings off of it. The easiest way to do this is to order these **flanges** from onboardair. [Post ID: 3835]
- Stainless braided line helps dissipate heat; at least 3ft of stainless line coming off the flanges is needed.[Post ID: 3835]

Maintenance and Additional Tips:
- Because you are converting what once was a closed system into an open system, oil needs to escape somewhere. There are a few options, including doing the **Oil Mod** or getting an oil separating unit from onboardair.com.[Post ID: 3835]

posts.original_html:
I have my compressor, now what do I need to get it mounted and in place?

Brackets:

You need to mount this thing somehow. Decide weather you want to run it off your alternator, in your serpentine belt rotation, or anywhere else (i have seen driveshaft, but not the best idea, lol).
Depeding on what you drive, you may or may not be in luck. Onboard Air and Air Ride Technologies sell brackets for popular applications. Mine was a 1988 4.3L OBS with a 4 groove serpentine setup. There were no
premanufactured brackets for my application, so i was forced to make my own. Remember when making your own brackets, that this thing needs to be solid! I cannot emphisize that enough. When this thing is pumping, there is some serious vibration.

Clutches:

You need to get the proper clutch set for your compressor. You need to decide how you will mount it, and that determines what clutches you will need.
If you want to run your york in your serpentine belt rotation, you will need a serpentine clutch . I have a V-belt clutch on my york, because i run
a Kilby Combo Pully


I have my york mounted, how do i plumb it?

You need to get some way of converting the rotolock thread flanges to NPT so you can run standard fittings off of it. The easiest way to do this is to order these flanges from onboardair. There are also flanges that screw over the exsisting rotolock thread.


Stainless Braided Line:
You NEED ATLEAST 3ft of stainless braided line coming off of the flanges. The air coming out of a york is very hot, and the stainless line helps dissapate the heat. I got 3 ft of stainless line from www.mcmaster.com. Cost = $36.
You can get the stainless line from ART, but i do not know the link.

Check Valve
The air coming out of a york is pressurized... duh. To prevent that pressure from coming back and blowing your york up, you need a check valve. You can get check valves just about anywhere. Try larry @ innovative or jason @ suicidedoors.


Fittings and other crap
I then run a compression fitting to run my DOT air line off of my check valve. This line then goes into a water trap, which goes into your air tank.
You also need an intake filter, because like anything else with a machined surface inside, you need to filter the air before it gets in.




Misc Crap to know about yorks


They spew alot of oil.
Because you are converting what once was a closed system into a open system, oil needs to escape somewhere. There are a few options, you can do the Oil Mod, or you can get an oil seperating unit from onboardair.com.
Read that Oil Mod link, as it is very informative.

Oil and maintence
Because of the oil escaping, you need the oil your compressor. I use 30W non-detergent oil, and a kilby dipstick to check to make sure it is full. A full compressor takes around 14 ounces of oil, and the kilby dipstick has a mark in it for every ounce of oil in the compressor.

Wiring
You wire your compressor is easy. With anything electrical, there are a few ways of doing it. I prefer mine to be manual, so i can control what RPM's my compressor comes on at, so i just wired a fuse inbetween the clutch wire and a switch that I use to turn the compressor on and off.
You can also use a pressure switch if you prefer, but make sure you use a relay. Do not hack wiring.




Here are some of the links that i used to help me with my setup:

http://www.geocities.com/spencerhut/truck/air.htm
http://www.universityofjeep.ca/oba_install_paul.html
http://moose.ca/~slowzuki/slowzuki/t...omp/OilFix.htm
http://www.jedi.com/obiwan/jeep/york_lube.html
http://www.ccicompressor.com/SrvcManl.htm
http://www.off-road.com/jeep/tech/body/york/
http://www.rockcrawler.com/techrepor...art1/york2.htm


Hope this thread helps... Add anything you feel necessary.
posts.rewritten_content:
To mount and install your compressor, you'll need brackets to secure it. Decide if you want to run the compressor off your alternator or in your serpentine belt rotation; homemade brackets may be necessary for some vehicles. For my 1988 4.3L OBS with a 4-groove serpentine setup, I had to create custom brackets due to the lack of pre-manufactured ones.

You must select the appropriate clutch based on your mounting location. A serpentine clutch is needed if you plan to use the compressor in this belt rotation; I used a V-belt clutch with my Kilby Combo Pulley.

To plumb the system, convert the rotolock thread flanges to NPT for standard fittings using brackets from Onboard Air or ART. For heat dissipation and to prevent excessive pressure, install at least 3 feet of stainless braided line and a check valve. Fittings should connect your check valve to the DOT air line leading into a water trap and then to your air tank.

An intake filter is essential for filtering air before it enters the system. The York compressor expels significant oil; consider an oil mod or oil separating unit from Onboard Air, as detailed in their documentation.

Regularly check the oil level with 30W non-detergent oil using a Kilby dipstick. A full compressor requires about 14 ounces of oil.

For wiring, I prefer a manual setup, adding a switch between the clutch wire and fuse for control over RPMs. Alternatively, use a pressure switch and relay if preferred. Ensure proper and safe electrical connections.

For more detailed information, refer to these resources:
- [Truck Air](http://www.geocities.com/spencerhut/truck/air.htm)
- [University of Jeep](http://www.universityofjeep.ca/oba_install_paul.html)

Today, I had to go into work due to an escaped prisoner and decided to use AutoTAP to gather data on my truck's Torque Management system. AutoTAP is a highly customizable program that provides detailed insights.

Why does your GM Truck lose power as it revs? And why is it slow after downshifting during wide open acceleration?

On an 03-04 GM truck, hitting the speed limiter shows:

- Ignition timing advance: Look great in Simple Idle mode.
- Wide open from a stop: Timing is pulled back and becomes negative.

This data demonstrates why Torque Management should be disabled.

ai_article.rewritten_title: NBS Big 3 Upgrade
ai_article.summary: The NBS Big 3 upgrade involves adding thicker wires to improve current flow and reduce voltage sag, which can help with dimming headlights. This is not a replacement of the factory wiring but an addition.
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
The NBS Big 3 upgrade involves adding thicker wires to improve current flow and reduce voltage sag, which can help with dimming headlights. This is not a replacement of the factory wiring but an addition.

This guide will walk you through the necessary components, costs, installation steps, and potential benefits.

### Required Components and Costs
- Battery positive to alternator wire (approx. 4’)
- Battery negative to chassis wire (approx. 4’)
- Engine block to chassis wire (approx. 5’)
- 4 ring terminals
- Heatshrink for covering the ring terminals
- Flex loom (not used in this system, as Stinger wire was sufficient)

Estimated total cost: $50-100, depending on the wire size/color and connector type.

Some users suggest using welding wire, which can be cheaper but may not look as nice.

### Installation Steps
- The red (+) goes to the alternator +. The silver (-) goes to a chassis bolt under the truck.
- The red (+) comes from the battery. The silver (-) is connected to the engine block just above the PS fluid reservoir and goes to a factory ground location on the firewall.

posts.rewritten_content: For older vehicles, adding a positive connection directly to the starter, while keeping grounds intact, could potentially benefit the alternator by providing additional charge. This might improve electrical system performance, enhance gas mileage in newer, computer-driven engines, and reduce the chance of the Check Engine Light (CEL) coming on. It could also bolster the stereo system and extend the life of components.

ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
The 4l60e transmission is a common component in many full-size trucks and vans. Proper identification of valvebody electronics can help diagnose issues, such as shifting problems and gear hold issues. NEUMANNZZ advises that the transmission should match the year and drivetrain type (2WD or 4WD) to ensure compatibility.

For instance, if a user has a 1995 truck with a 2WD configuration, they can expect to face clutch-related issues like losing power during shifting. NEUMANNZZ suggests that these transmissions should be rebuilt locally due to their unique nature.

Additionally, users reported intermittent shifting problems and gear hold failures after rebuilding or replacing components. Code 67 related to the torque converter clutch (TCC) solenoid was discussed, indicating a potential issue with this circuit causing electrical problems inside the transmission. NEUMANNZZ recommends using a multimeter to test the TCC circuit and other relevant signals like speed sensor (VSS), engine RPMs (tach signal on the coil).

For those considering swapping transmissions, NEUMANNZZ provides detailed wiring diagrams for both 4l60e and 4l80e models. He advises ensuring that all components are replaced during transmission rebuild to avoid future issues.

posts.original_html: Ok another thing i can check is to see if the vcm is actually grounding out the solenoids to make it shift. How would I go about checking that?
posts.rewritten_content:
To verify if the VCM is properly grounding the solenoids for shifting, you can use a multimeter to test the electrical connection between the VCM and the solenoids. Ensure the system is turned off and follow these steps:

1. Locate the relevant connections.
2. Set your multimeter to the continuity or diode test mode.
3. Touch one probe to the VCM terminal and the other to the solenoid terminal.
4. Check for a solid connection.

If no connection is detected, there may be an issue with the grounding.

seo_outline: Examples of Lift Kits and Tires Used
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
This thread showcases various lifted two-wheel drive (2WD) setups for Chevrolet Silverado trucks, highlighting the modifications made by forum members and how they use their vehicles. Users share details such as lift kit size, tire and wheel specifications, and intended applications like daily driving or off-roading.

### Examples of Lift Kits and Tires Used
- **Chuggs (2006 Silverado 98):** Rancho 4" lift with rear add-a-leafs, 33-12.50-15 BFG mud terrains, 15X8 black rock crawler rims, Thrush glasspack mufflers w/turndowns, grillguard, and 2-130 watt Explorer Procomp lights in the front.
- **metalhead (98 Silverado):** Rancho 4" lift with a 7" total lift at the end, 32x11.50 BFG tires, and stock 15X10 hurricanes wheels. Gear down from 3.42 to 4.11 for better performance and gas mileage.
- **TampaCCSB (2006 Silverado):** 7" Fabtech crossmember system lift with 325/60/18 tires, 18x10 wheels with 4.5" backspacing.
- **02slvrdo86 (02 Silverado):** RC 3" spindle lift and a 3" body lift with 285/75/16 tires and 16x8 wheels with 4.5" backspacing.
- **BigBlue2wd (03 Silverado):** 12" total lift using a 7" Fabtech drop down kit, a 3" Performance Acc. Body Lift, and a 2" Front Coil Spacer (with caution).
- **kutter79 (2005 Silverado):** CST 4" spindle lift with 265/70/17 tires and OEM 17" wheels and .5" wheel spacers in the front.

### Usage and Intended Applications
- Chuggs mainly uses his truck for offroading, while TampaCCSB uses it mostly on roads but occasionally goes to the beach or flooded areas. 
- metalhead mentions a 4x4 setup as a future goal due to the lack of gear reduction.
- BigBlue2wd enjoys both road and off-road use, with no issues clearing his tires.

I installed the Rancho 4/2 lift on my truck two years ago, along with 32x11.50 BFG tires. The original stock rear shackles were replaced with drop shackles initially, using 295/50 BFGs. After the lift, the total front lift is 7 inches and the rear lift is 4 inches. I reverted to the stock rear shackles after lifting.

A year ago, I changed the gear ratio from stock 3.42s to 4.11s, which significantly improved acceleration and increased fuel efficiency by about 2 mpg, bringing it back close to its original performance levels.

ai_article.rewritten_title: Before & After Projects Showcase
ai_article.summary: This thread features various members sharing images of their Fullsize Chevrolet trucks and cars from the time they were purchased to after major modifications, allowing others to seek inspiration for their own vehicles.
seo_outline: Introduction to a 'before and after' thread concept
Examples of before and after transformations
Suggestions and recommendations from other members
ai_article.rewritten_article_markdown:
The idea of creating an official 'before and after' thread for Fullsize Chevrolet trucks and cars was proposed by GMCTruck21. The thread is meant to showcase the changes made to vehicles over time, providing a visual guide for those looking to modify their own trucks or cars.

GMCTruck21 shared images of his 2002 GMC Sierra from March 1, 2010, and October 10, 2011. He stated that he wished the truck retained more of its original OEM style look: 

- *Before* (March 1, 2010): ![Truck on date of purchase](http://i275.photobucket.com/albums/jj286/Lukeizzle991/My%202002%20GMC%20Sierra/IMAGE_105.jpg)
- *After* (October 10, 2011): ![Truck as of October 10, 2011](http://i275.photobucket.com/albums/jj286/Lukeizzle991/IMAG0774.jpg)

Other members contributed their own 'before and after' projects. For instance, custm2500 suggested that the bumper and cap should be rino lined to match the rockers.

- *Before*: ![Truck before modifications](http://i354.photobucket.com/albums/r418/Minimeh1993/96%20GMC%20pics/004.jpg)
- *After*: ![Truck after modifications](http://i354.photobucket.com/albums/r418/Minimeh1993/IMG_0097.jpg), ![Truck after additional modifications](http://i354.photobucket.com/albums/r418/Minimeh1993/IMG_0100.jpg)

Another example was provided by probuilder1, who shared images of his truck before and after waxing:
- *Before*: ![Probuilder1's truck before wax](http://i251.photobucket.com/albums/gg299/probuilder1/Truck.jpg)
- *After*: ![Probuilder1's truck after wax](http://i251.photobucket.com/albums/gg299/probuilder1/waxed2.jpg)

Members also provided feedback, with GMCTruck21 praising probuilder1 for the result.
